content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work introduce a two-stage encoder for 3D generative NeRF inversion. A base encoder is firstly employed to invert a coarse latent code. An identity contrastive learning is used to preserve 3D consistent novel view images, by leveraging synthesized multi-view images of the same identity. Then,  a residual encoder is adopted to refine the latent code to yield finer inversion results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The paper is well organized and the overall idea is clear and easy to follow.

Weaknesses:
1. The contribution of this work is limited. Most inversion techniques in this work have been explored in previous 2D inversion, e.g., residual inversion used ReStyle. This work tends to adapt the encoder-based 2D inversion methods to 3D GANs, there is some special design in this paper but the novelty is still not strong.

2. The effectiveness of the triplet loss in eq. (6) is not clearly validated. The experiments only validate the effectiveness of $x_{syn}$ and $L_{feat_{syn}}$. As $L_{feat_{syn}}$ consists of two terms, it is not clear that the gain comes from the $L_1$ or triplet loss $L_{tri}$. This ablation is necessary as the triplet loss is main (even only) interesting point compared with existing inversion methods for my understanding.
Besides, I have concern about the effectiveness of $L_{tri}$, as it is too easy to distinguish positive & negative pairs for human faces, especially considering there already is a clear $L_{1}$ objective for inversion in eq. (7).

3. Some results are not very convincing. Fig. 1 (c) shows that the inversion result of single-view only is very bad. However, based on my own experience and experiments, inverting a single-view image can also produce meaningful results for StyleNeRF and will not be so bad as presented in the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The overall clarity and quality of this work is ok, but the novelty is not good enough. 
There are some issues for reproducibility. See Strength And Weaknesses for more detail.
content.summary_of_the_review: The overall contribution & novelty of this work is not strong enough as most techniques have been explored in previous research of 2D inversion. The effectiveness of triplet loss is not clearly validated.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4ayG
content.comment:
We thank you for the constructive suggestions. We now address the raised issues below:

1) To weakness 1
We disagree that the contribution is limited. Though several techniques are from the previous works, the novelty of our model lies in how we build the two-stage encoders. We introduce 1) a base encoder to learn the view-invariant latent code in W space and 2) residual encoder to refine the latent codes. We would like to note that, the key design of our model is the base encoder which produces “well 3D preservation view-invariant latent code” as a valid starting point. The second stage is actually less important compared with first-stage encoder. While the second stage encoder is inspired by Restyle, Restyle only learns W+ residual starting from “the average W+ latent” which will fail to preserve 3D shape through several iterations. Instead, our model learns the residues starting from the closest view-invariant W+ latent. We also would like to note that again, it is not trivial to directly apply existing inversion models such as Restyle directly since these models do not consider the 3D preservation. As shown from Figure 5 and the demo video, Restyle and other well-known models fail to produce 3D faces while both Restyle and our model utilize residual learning. We are also the first to propose plug-and-play encoder-based inversion for style-based NeRFs.

2) To weakness 2
The ablations on the triplet loss and L2 loss are included in the Figure 6 of edited main paper now. We think the $L_{tri}$ may not be easy to optimize since it will need to ensure the latent derives from the same identities yet with different poses are close, which is not trivial.

3) To weakness 3
We think that inverting a single-view image is not trivial to produce a satisfactory result. If we apply the current online inversion method (PTI) using the perceptual and L2 loss for example, it will only optimize this single-view rendered with specific camera pose while other novel-view results will not be optimized. This is caused by 3D depth ambiguity and you can always generate the same single-view rendered results with different 3D shapes. This is also why we utilize our first-stage encoder to produce the view-invariant representation first then perform following optimization techniques. We also include the tsne latent project in figure 1 of the edited manuscript (please download the manuscript it again) which shows our base encoder plus residual learning is able to obtain the closest W+ latent to the original StyleNeRF latent manifold.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work is about the task of GAN inversion to tame a new encoder for a pre-trained generative model. Unlike most existing works that perform the GAN inversion in 2D, here the authors aim to do the 3D GAN inversion utilizing the latest 3D generators, such as StyleNeRF, StyleSDF and EG3D. To achieve this goal, two encoders are proposed for the base latent feature and refined latent estimating, respectively. Besides, the authors introduce the contrastive learning to ensure the 3D consistent for the same identity. Experiments are conducted on face datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
#### **Strengths**
- The 3D GAN inversion is interesting, which is significant for unsupervised 3D reconstruction that learns 3D models from large collected 2D images, instead of collecting 3D models in the real world.
- The overall idea and the proposed mapping method towards addressing the latent representation is reasonable. The StyleNeRF and EG3D are the powerful 3D face generators. This is exactly suitable for exploring the 2D-to-3D mapping.
- In the experiment, the claimed 3D visual results are being met.

#### **Weaknesses**
While the authors aim to address a challenging and novel task, I believe some parts need more clarification (even after considering the supplementary material and video):
- The biggest weakness is that the proposed method has limited novelty. While the authors propose two encoders and contrastive learning to address the 3D inconsistent issue, the key contribution they made is unclear.
    - Contrastive loss is an interesting loss to ensure the 3D consistency. However, it takes me a hard time to search the significance of this loss. If this loss is a contribution, the authors should demonstrate it in the experiment.
    - The two stage encoder has been widely used in the 2D GAN inversion. What's the difference to the existing methods?
- The authors claimed "3DE-NeRF is the first 3D-aware encoder for generative style-based NeRFs". However, the prior works [r1,r2,r3] has explored the 2D-to-3D mapping using a pretrained generator. In particular, the IDE-3D also claimed they are the 3D-aware GAN inversion. The authors should compare with these highly related works, or at least discuss them.
- For the GAN inversion, the most important part is mapping the input data to the same latent space (w or z space) of the pretrained generators. The authors may utilize the t-SNE method as mentioned in [r4, r5] to demonstrate the proposed method learns a better mapping architecture. 
- The identity information in Figures 4 and 5 are lost. The outputs are very different to the input identity.
- The visual results of "w+ opt" in figures 4 and 5 are ambiguity, but why the quantitative score in Table 1 is good for L2?

[r1] Chen, Anpei, et al. "Sofgan: A portrait image generator with dynamic styling." ACM Transactions on Graphics (TOG) 41.1 (2022): 1-26.
 
[r2] Sun, Jingxiang, et al. "IDE-3D: Interactive Disentangled Editing for High-Resolution 3D-aware Portrait Synthesis." Siggraph Asia (2022).

[r3] Chen, Yuedong, et al. "Sem2NeRF: Converting Single-View Semantic Masks to Neural Radiance Fields." ECCV (2022).

[r4] Song, Guoxian, et al. "AgileGAN: stylizing portraits by inversion-consistent transfer learning." ACM Transactions on Graphics (TOG) 40.4 (2021): 1-13.

[r5] Wu, Zongze, et al. "Stylealign: Analysis and applications of aligned stylegan models." ICLR (2022).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
#### **Clarity**
- The paper is well organized and easy to follow. 
- The key motivation and overall idea toward addressing the task is clearly explained.

#### **Quality**
- The reconstructed 3D model is limited, and the 3D view consistent is not well visualized.
- The authors only compare with the 2D GAN inversion methods.

#### **Novelty**
- The key novelty in the paper is the novel task, while the network configuration and loss function are borrowed from existing works.
- However, this novel task has been explored by some highly related works (IDE-3D and Sem2NeRF), which are published or released before the ICLR deadline. The authors should compare with these state-of-the-art methods, or at least discuss the difference between them.

#### **Reproducibility**
- While the code is not provided, I believe the experimental results can be reproduced using the methods mentioned by the authors.
content.summary_of_the_review: My preliminary rating for this submission is reject. While I like the novel task that aims to mapping 2D image to 3D representation using a pre-trained 3D generator, the key novelty and contribution are unclearly explained with the prior related works. Neither the proposed network configuration nor the losses are new. In additional, compared with the latest 2D-to-3D mapping works, the proposed works seem to perform worse than other related works. The authors should compare with these highly related works, or at lease discuss the difference between them.

content.title: Response to Reviewer WnNs
content.comment:
We thank you for the constructive suggestions. We now address the raised issues below:

1) To weakness 1:
a) The ablations on the triplet loss and L2 loss are included in the Figure 6 of the edited main paper now. b) We disagree that the proposed method has limited novelty. Though several techniques are from the previous works, the novelty of our model lies in how we build the two-stage encoders. We introduce 1) a base encoder to learn the "view-invariant latent code" in W+ space and 2) residual encoder to refine the latent codes. We would like to note that, the key design of our model is the base encoder which produces “well 3D preservation view-invariant latent code” as a valid starting point. The second stage is actually less important compared with first-stage encoder. While the second stage encoder is inspired by Restyle, Restyle only learns W+ residual starting from “the average W+ latent” which will fail to preserve 3D shape through several iterations. Instead, our model learns the residues starting from the closest view-invariant W+ latent. We also would like to note that again, it is not trivial to directly apply existing inversion models such as Restyle directly since these models do not consider the 3D preservation. As shown from Figure 5 and the demo video, Restyle and other well-known models fail to produce 3D faces while both Restyle and our model utilize residual learning.

2) To weakness 2:
While we realize our claim may bring such confusion in the problem formulation, our GAN inversion is strictly formulated as: given only a single face image from a person, we aim to render the multi-view images from the same identity using the pre-trained generator. Therefore, the task of [r1,r3] is to generate 3D faces using the 2D input semantic map which is different from our task. On the other hand, the GAN inversion of [r2] requires both input image and “a semantic map”, which can not be generalized to typical GAN inversion with single input image. Also ,the inversion model in [r2] can only be applied to their designed model taking into both semantic maps. Hence, we would like to note that again, our model is currently the only inversion model which can serve as plug-and-play to many existing latent-guided style-based NeRF models such as StyleNeRF, Eg3D, GRAM, StyleSDF, … and so on. We have included the citations of [r1,r2,r3] into the related works for discussion: [r1,r3] in the section of "Image Synthesis with Generative NeRF" and [r2] in the section of "GAN inversion".

3) To weakness 3:
We have included the tsne projection on W+ StyleNeRF space following [r4] in the Figure 1 of the updated paper. This tsne figure shows our base encoder plus residual learning is able to obtain the closest W+ latent to the original StyleNeRF latent manifold compared to other general inversion models (pSp and Restyle).

4) To weakness 4:
We agree that the identity reconstruction is not that perfect in Figure 4 and Figure 5. However, compared with the other strong baseline encoder-based models and even online-based methods (which optimize the latent code for each sample individually), our two-stage encoders preserve the best 3D face structure and the closest identity details for novel-views without further online tuning. We also show that the latent derived using our encoder can be refined further with online optimization and make it perfect (see Figure 10 and demo video). In terms of the perfect reconstruction for NeRF, we propose the only one pipeline (our model + PTI refinement) which can produce perfect inversion.

5) To weakness 5:
The samples we picked in Figure 4 and Figure 5 are difficult cases in which the inversion is not easy to be performed even with online-based methods (optimize each sample individually). Yet, the L2 score is computed over the testing set thus the quantitative score in Table 1 is better than the encoder-based score for single-view reconstruction.

Let us know if you have more concerns.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper aims to invert well-trained 3D-aware GANs for the novel-view synthesis of real images.
The authors propose a two-stage encoder to alleviate challenging problems of 3D inversion.
Besides, a contrastive loss is introduced for better 3D consistency. 
The method is mainly evaluated with StyleNeRF on FFHQ dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I think inverting 3D GAN is a good problem, and the author has a reasonable solution to accomplish it.
However, the results and experimental results are not comprehensive to support its effectiveness.

Strengths:
The contrastive learning strategy is interesting, which is helpful in improving multi-view consistency of the inverted images.

Weakness:
1. I think the author does not clarify their experimental setting. How do you infer the poses of the real images? Have you adopted the dataset with pose annotation? I think it is very important for this task. Because if you know the camera pose, the problem will be easier because inferring an accurate 3D pose from a single image is challenging without any prior model. Maybe you can predict accurate poses in the face dataset with 3DMM, but it is very difficult to perform it on complex datasets like compcars.
2. I assume poses can be inferred accurately with the encoder. However, potentially StyleNeRF is not a good model for 3D inversion, because it suffers from pose unalignment in the canonical space. It means when you infer different latents with the same camera pose, synthesized images' poses are slightly different. And this bad property makes your encoder confusing during optimization, harming your experimental results.  
3. Besides results in Section 4, I also checked the EG3D results provided in supplementary materials. The inversion quality is not very good.
As shown in Figure 4, 3rd sample struggles to keep the expression, and 4-th sample suffers from the hair and color consistent. 
4. The technical novelty is limited. Several technicals are similar to previous work， like residual encoder.
5. The inference time should be included in fair comparison because this method uses two encoders and sequential testing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I think this paper is present well, and the topic explored in this paper is interesting. 
However, the quality of the results is not very good. I hope the authors can further improve their methods.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1pb3
content.comment:
Thank you for the constructive suggestions. We now address the raised issues below:

1) To weakness 1:
As we have stated in section 4.1 in the paper that “the camera poses for all real input are derived using the off-the-shelf pose estimator: HopeNet (Ruiz et al., 2018) for a fair comparison with previous works.” Yet, compared with the baseline models: W encoder, pSp, Restyle, as well as the online optimization methods, our model does not require off-the-shelf pose predictor since our first-stage encoder will produce the camera pose automatically.

2) To weakness 2:
We agree that StyleNeRF suffers from pose unalignment in the canonical space. For example, StyleNeRF can always generate a facial frontal view head pose with the slightly wrong camera pose. Yet, since we can still generate a facial frontal view with wrong camera pose using StyleNeRF and perform novel-view synthesis to rotate the head, this means StyleNeRF is more robust for 3D inversion with incorrect pose. We compare StyleNeRF with EG3D and found that this is the reason why 3D NeRF-inversion works much better than Eg3D while Eg3D has better pose alignment. On the other hand, our method also works for EG3D and possibly also works for other existing generators such as GRAM, StyleSDF, or so. In brief, our model is able to serve as a plug-and-play tool.

3) To weakness 3:
We also observe that the inversion is not easier for Eg3D than StyleNeRF and we credit the reason that the latent manifold in Eg3D does not generalize to unseen faces well while their cat face is very easy to be inverted (Figure 16).
We agree that the inversion quality is not that perfect in Figure 4. However, compared with the other strong baseline encoder-based models and even online-based methods (which optimize the latent code for each sample individually), our two-stage encoders preserve the best 3D face structure and the closest identity details for novel-views without further online tuning. We would appreciate it if you could take a look at the demo video (inside the supplementary zip file) which has the most obvious rendered results than the figures in the paper. Our model is the only one model preserving good 3D shape and the closest identity in the comparisons with ALL other candidate models.

4) To weakness 4:
Though several techniques are from the previous works, the novelty of our model lies in how we build the two-stage encoders. We introduce 1) a base encoder to learn the "view-invariant latent code" in W+ space and 2) residual encoder to refine the latent codes. We would like to note that, the key design of our model is the base encoder which produces “well 3D preservation view-invariant latent code” as a valid starting point. The second stage is actually less important compared with first-stage encoder.
While the second stage encoder is inspired by Restyle, Restyle only learns W+ residual starting from “the average W+ latent” which will fail to preserve 3D shape through several iterations. Instead, our model learns the residues starting from the closest view-invariant W+ latent. We also would like to note that again, it is not trivial to directly apply existing inversion models such as Restyle directly since these models do not consider the 3D preservation. As shown from Figure 5 and the demo video, Restyle fails to produce 3D faces while both Restyle and our model utilize residual learning. We also include the tsne latent project in figure 1 of the edited manuscript (please download the manuscript it again) which shows our base encoder plus residual learning is able to obtain the closest W+ latent to the original StyleNeRF latent manifold.

4) To weakness 5:
We summarize the the inference time for one sample at:

| Model           | Inference time (s)            |
|-----------------|-------------------------------|
| W encoder       |          0.105 (s)            |
| pSp             |          0.132 (s)            |
| Restyle         |          0.454 (s)            |
| 3DE-NeRF (ours) |          0.315 (s)            |
| W+ optimize     |        194.203 (s)            |
| PTI             |         66.153 (s)            |

Since our model is an encoder-based model, the inference time of our model is much faster than the online-based model and even faster than Restyle which utilizes five iterations. We have also revised the paper by including the time into the table.

content.title: Response to all of the reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all of the reviewers for the constructive feedback and we have edited the manuscript as follows:

1. We have included the tsne W+ latent projection and comparisons in the Figure 1 of the paper.
2. We have included the citations of [r1,r2,r3] suggested by reviewer WnNs into the related works for discussion: [r1,r3] in the section of "Image Synthesis with Generative NeRF" and [r2] in the section of "GAN inversion".
3. We have included the inference time for each model in Table 1.
4. We have included the ablation on $L_{tri}$ and $L_{2}$ in Figure 6 as well as the discussion in section 4.4.

We have responded to each of reviewer respectively and we now summarize our response to the two major common concerns: 1) Novelty and 2) Rendering quality:

1. Regarding the novelty:
We would like to emphasize that the novelty of our model lies in that our first-stage encoder learns a well 3D preservation view-invariant latent with contrastive learning as a good starting point. The second stage encoder is just for further refinement and is not the key design we would like to put emphasis on. As shown from Figure 5 and the demo video, Restyle fails to produce 3D faces (more like flat faces) without a good starting point while our model is able to produce 3D-aware faces with the same residual learning. The updated tsne in figure 1 also supports the importance of our first-stage encoder. In addition, the idea of view-invariant learning never shows in previous inversion methods since their models are not designed for latent-based generative NeRFs which assume the w latent is strongly to be view-invariant.


2. Regarding the rendering quality:
We realize that the results in Figure 4 and Figure 5 are not satisfactory while we picked the difficult cases in these two figures. Since our model is designed as an encoder-based approach, it usually can not produce perfect reconstruction if it has never seen the input face during the training. However, interestingly compared with online-optimized methods (PTI) which is usually the upper bound of the encoder-based, our method exhibits superior quality than it and other baseline approaches. We achieve the best quality of novel-view rendering quantitatively shown in Table 2. The latent derived using our encoder can be further refined with online-based methods yet we do not put it in Figure 4 and Figure 5 just for fair comparison.
Furthermore, to produce the “perfect” reconstruction and novel-view rendering, we do actually propose to combine our model with PTI which can lead to perfect inversion results (see “ours + PTI” in the Figure 10 and demo video). We are currently the only model that can potentially perform perfect NeRF inversion with online optimization.

We hope reviewers can re-evaluate our paper based on our response.
